questions.q: What is the difference between a primary theme and a secondary theme in a literary work?
questions.a: A primary theme is the central, dominating idea of the work (e.g., adolescent fantasising in "Going Places"), while secondary themes are supporting ideas that run parallel, adding depth and complexity (e.g., socio-economic constraints, family dynamics). A wrong answer would treat all themes as equal or confuse a plot detail (like the biscuit factory) with a theme (class limitations). This reveals the student cannot distinguish hierarchical thematic structure.

questions.q: In "Going Places," Sophie's father is described as having a "plump face still grimy and sweat-marked from the day" and eating "shepherd's pie as hard as he could go." What secondary theme do these details support, and how?
questions.a: These details support the secondary theme of socio-economic constraints/working-class reality. The physical description shows manual labour exhaustion; the hurried eating suggests no leisure time. A wrong answer would say "it shows he loves food" or "it shows he's messy," missing the thematic function. This reveals the student cannot connect physical description to thematic purpose.

questions.q: Jansie says, "They don't pay well for shop work, you know that, your dad would never allow it." Sophie thinks Jansie is "nosey" and "gawky." Analyse how this contrast between Jansie and Sophie serves the secondary theme of friendship and trust.
questions.a: Jansie represents pragmatic acceptance of their shared destiny (biscuit factory), while Sophie sees this as betrayal of their friendship. The contrast highlights how class solidarity (Jansie) clashes with individual escape fantasies (Sophie), making trust fragile. A wrong answer would only describe their personalities without linking to theme. This reveals the student cannot analyse character contrast as thematic device.

questions.q: Geoff's silence is described as "words had to be prized out of him like stones out of the ground." Sophie is "jealous of his silence" because "when he wasn't speaking it was as though he was away somewhere... out there in the world." Explain how Geoff's silence functions as a symbol for the secondary theme of adolescent longing for escape.
questions.a: Geoff's silence symbolises the inaccessible adult world Sophie craves. His physical presence but emotional absence makes him a portal to the "vast world out there." The metaphor "stones out of the ground" suggests his world is hard-won, real, and closed to her. A wrong answer would say "Geoff is shy" or "they don't talk much," missing the symbolic function. This reveals the student cannot interpret metaphor as thematic symbol.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Sophie's meeting with Danny Casey in the arcade is the only 'real' event in the story; everything else is her imagination." Use evidence from the text to defend or refute.
questions.a: The statement is false. The arcade meeting is itself imagined — the text reveals this when Sophie waits by the canal and "imagined his coming," then admits "he will not come." The only real events are the family dinner, the football match, and Jansie's conversation. A wrong answer would claim the meeting really happened, missing the story's structural irony. This reveals the student cannot distinguish narrative layers (fantasy vs. reality) — a core analytical skill.

questions.q: Write a 4-line diary entry from Sophie's perspective the night after she waits by the canal, capturing the secondary theme of "the burden of unprovable truth."
questions.a: A strong entry: "Geoff believes me. Dad doesn't. Jansie would mock me. But I know what happened — his green eyes, the freckles, the promise. The truth is mine alone, heavy as a stone in my pocket. Tomorrow I'll pretend I never waited." A weak entry would focus only on sadness or Danny Casey, missing the thematic weight of unverifiable private truth. This reveals the student cannot synthesise theme into creative voice.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Secondary themes are the underlying ideas that run parallel to the primary theme, enriching the narrative by exploring related social, ______, or emotional dimensions.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're watching a movie where the main character dreams of becoming a superstar, but every scene shows their cramped apartment, tired parents, and friends who say "be realistic." That's "Going Places" — Sophie's fantasies are the main plot, but the secondary themes are the ______ details that make her dreams both understandable and heartbreaking.
What is Secondary themes? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Secondary themes are the underlying ideas that run parallel to the primary theme, enriching the narrative by exploring related social, psychological, or emotional dimensions.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Secondary themes?
questions.a: Students often treat every topic mentioned in the story (football, boutique, biscuit factory, motorcycle) as a separate theme.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify at least three secondary themes in "Going Places," provide textual evidence for each, and explain how each secondary theme interacts with the primary theme of adolescent fantasising to deepen the story's meaning.
